elements.content: *If you know where to look

slides.notes:
These are actual warnings 

Point out the version numbers: 12.0.0 and 13.0.0.

Fun part: you won't see these. Core raises them with @trigger_error(), so they never hit dblog or the screen. This is so that your dblog doesn't get full of deprecation notices in prod, so I had to write my own set_error_handler() to catch them. The way these warnings are captured are silent at runtime, but they surface in tests and static analysis

form_alter, preprocess_node, entity_presave, cron, help, page_attachments, mail_alter, node_access: zero deprecation notices.

So the hooks you have the most of are the ones that don't warn you. This is why "wait and see" is a bad plan.

Now let's take a look at a basic hook migration.  No code, just the wrapper.

A standard hook.  One that most of us have probably used with some regularity.  It's warm, it's familiar, and it makes you feel good inside.
I know it's hard to say goodbye, but don't worry, it's replacement will feel just as Drupally as this one, but with a modern flair!
Change is scary.  I know.  It is hard to say goodbye to yesterday, but don't worry... it's still the Drupal we all know and love.

See?  It's not too bad, right?  We still name the hook, we still have the same arguments, it's just more modern and, in my opinion, cleaner.

Let's look inside a hook class

items: No services.yml needed: core registers and autowires it

slides.notes:
Group by what the hooks deal with, not one giant MymoduleHooks class. One giant class is just a .module file with extra steps.
File location: should live in `module/src/Hook` and you can make it even more granular if you want

Namespace: Needs to match the module + folder name so that it gets autoloaded.  If you went more granular it might be Drupal\mymodule\Hook\Entity. 

Classname: I'm using standard Drupal naming conventions with the format Modulename Type Hooks. Now, you can name this anything you like, but the classname needs to match the filename or it won't get picked up correctly.

The attribute: This is where the magic is.  ANY public method in the class can be prefixed with a hook attribute and act as that hook

By using classes... technically services, we inject through the class constructor instead of the global \Drupal:: class

Point out the docblock: it says hook_node_presave, but the function is entity_presave. Nobody noticed for years because Drupal doesn't read docblocks. Rector does. Plant this, pay it off later.

This is what I love about this.  Before, a function was named generically and you have to count on comments, documentation, or often just your failing memory (maybe that's just me?) to figure out what was going on.

Now, we break it out into 3 different methods that we can name for what they actually do!

The best part of the migration, in my opinion. Same hook, three methods, and the names tell you what they do. The underscore helper becomes an actual private method.

The overview first, then the full code on the next two slides.

items: Skipped entity_presave: the docblock named the wrong hook

slides.notes:
When I ran it on my fake real module that wasn't based on anything I'd ever write ever, there were mixed results.
It did convert most of the functions, but Rector finds hooks by the docblock, not the function name. Remember the wrong docblock from earlier? That didn't get fixed
If there's no docblock at all, it definitely won't find and convert the function.
It also didn't take into account the version for the module in the .info and wrote a shim and wrote a services file for the new classes.  This isn't horrible, but it's unnecessary in 11.3+ and ends up being manual cleanup.

The --clear-cache one is the scariest: green output, zero changes.
If you run rector once to clean up deprecations, the module's files get cached.  If you do a second pass to do the hook conversion without the clear-cache flag, it'll report green and nothing will have changed.

Let's take a look at how rector handled this as of mid October

One big class for everything. No types. Fully qualified names inline. PSR-2 braces, not Drupal standards.

Grouped class, types (nullable where core passes NULL), Drupal formatting, explicit return.

Verdict: Rector is a decent first draft if your docblocks are honest. Plan to rewrite what it gives you. And always run it with --clear-cache.

This is what Rector left in .module. #[LegacyHook] keeps the procedural function for older cores that don't know about hook classes, and newer cores skip it.

You need this only if your module still supports cores where hook classes don't work. Contrib maintainers are probably going to use these a lot, but for your own custom code that's on 11.3+, no: delete it.
